articles.title: Clearing the air
articles.content: THE morning after we landed in London three weeks ago, my nine-year-old and I went out for a walk post-breakfast. Out of nowhere, she said “Baba, I can breathe here.” I looked at her: she had a big smile on her face. She was not making a political or ideological statement; she was just making a statement of fact about the air. Living in Lahore, over the last two to three years we had gotten her used to wearing a mask all the time when outside. In London, I could see her face when we were walking that morning. I checked the Air Quality Index for London right after her remark: it was 20. I checked what the AQI in Lahore was at the time: it was 140. As I write this article, the AQI in London is 55 and around 150 in Lahore. The average AQI for Lahore last year was around 170. We had many days when the AQI was in the 200-300 range. For London, it was 42 in 2024 and 45 in 2025. Despite the fact that my daughter had to wear a mask whenever she was out in the open in Lahore, she still had to take medication containing montelukast sodium, which is commonly used for allergies and managing respiratory issues like asthma. It has been more of a friend to her over the last few years — a period in which she has been far sicker than in the first five to six years of her life — than any of her classmates. This was also the case with other children in her class and school. A paediatrician told me that children in Pakistan seemed to be living on this particular medicine — at least much more than on chocolates or other sweets. School absences on account of sickness have risen as well. We have yet to see a major sustained effort to reduce air pollution in the country. There is no dearth of evidence regarding the deleterious impact of air pollution on human health. In children, lung development as well as brain and cognitive development, are impacted. In adults, sustained exposure to air pollution increases the risk of heart disease, blood pressure, strokes, dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other respiratory issues. In some places, hospitals gear up for surges in the number of patients coming in with specific complaints (heart attacks in the elderly, etc) if the air quality is poor and has been poor for some time. Long-term exposure to air pollution has a significant impact on the health and longevity of all, but it has a more serious impact on children as their capacities are still developing. London had come a long way from the days of the London smog. But it was still not enough. So, in 2019, despite widespread scepticism and stiff opposition from many quarters, the mayor of London sanctioned the implementation of the Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) programme. It was eventually expanded to all London boroughs. Under the programme, vehicles had to meet stricter emission guidelines or pay stiff fines. Since it raised costs for vehicle users and owners, it was not popular but a recent five-year study has shown the significant impact it has had on children’s health. According to the study, ULEZ is strongly associated with accelerated and restored lung function growth in children. The study compared children in London with children in Luton. Both had comparable air quality rules to start with, but Luton did not come under ULEZ. At the start of the study, London’s children had significantly smaller lungs than their peers in Luton. But over five years, children in London caught up with those in Luton and the proportion of children with clinically impaired lung function dropped by five per cent. A separate study showed that over 2019-2024, deaths linked to toxic air fell by about 40pc alongside a 41pc drop in nitrogen dioxide in London. Scepticism about ULEZ has gone down. There are a number of British cities that are now implementing or contemplating the implementation of similar programmes. The mayor of London recently said that the implementation of ULEZ was the hardest decision he had to make as mayor but the results have shown it was needed and that the children of London were reaping the rewards now. Heating systems in Sofia — the capital of Bulgaria — were very dependent on coal and wood burning. These are being replaced as part of a citywide clean air programme, which includes a subsidy for low-income groups. Results already show an approximately 20pc reduction in the emission of harmful particulates. It is not just cities in rich countries that have done this or are doing it. London, Paris and Barcelona may be good examples of what can be done in just a few years, but it is cities in the not-so-rich countries that are also cleaning up the air or have plans to do so, because the cost of inaction is far too high. Bogotá — the capital of Colombia — is doing more work in this area. It has cut air pollution by about 24pc since 2018. The Kenyan capital of Nairobi passed an air quality law in 2022 that commits to cutting harmful emission by half by 2035. Hundreds of cities are embarking on the journey to clean up the environment. There is a lot of discussion of these issues in Pakistan whenever we have a season of high AQI numbers and schools are closed and emergency action is taken to address pollution. But we have not seen major medium- to long-term initiatives to take us to a place where the lungs and brains are not impacted by pollutants in the air, and where medication is not our children’s best friend. Though resolute and comprehensive action requires significant state buy-in and commitment, we also need a lot of citizen action to motivate and push the state. On both fronts, we need much more work and attention. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
articles.author: Faisal Bari

articles.title: A polity or petri dish?
articles.content: CONTRARY to the interior minister’srecent claim, bad governance is not the cause of the recurring collapse of political systems. It is only a symptom of a deeper systemic malaise — an undemocratic dispensation that allows the rulers to escape political and institutional accountability for their ills and excesses. The minister’s panacea for bad governance — the creation of more provinces — is also misconceived, if not potentially disastrous for a country already riddled with multiple fault lines. Enforcing central authority over multiple sub-national units has become increasingly difficult for authoritarian states or contested governments. Nigeria, Afghanistan, Sudan, Libya, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Somalia are some of the many countries that have a large number of provinces; yet they are perennially afflicted with bad governance, fractious territories, economic meltdowns, civil wars, armed insurgencies and institutional breakdowns. The genesis of our systemic maladies can also be traced to a combination of undemocratic and authoritarian models that have been tried for decades on various pretexts — ideology, faith, stability, security, integrity, development, etc — to elude a legitimate federal democracy. Therefore, the answer to key political questions regarding the state’s foundational objectives, system of governance, people’s rights and liberties, and the distribution of resources within the federation and among the people has never been attempted. These are basic questions that the first generation of a political leadership must respond to, by way of a social compact that secures legitimacy, recognition, order and cohesion for the newborn state. Else, these questions hover over regicide, fratricide and every revolt or revolution. The common thread running through all successful social compacts is the ‘will of the people’. The people are the bedrock of modern states. They constitute the foundation of the state and work and sustain it with their blood and sweat. No polity can stand, let alone perform, without the people as the object and drivers of state-building. But it is unfortunate that right after independence, a small coterie of elites — political, business, landed and the civil-military establishment — captured power and diverted resources towards their own political and institutional interests. Constitution-making remained stalled for many years. And then in 1954, a mentally incapacitated governor-general dissolved the first elected constituent assembly, which had just finished the draft of the constitution, because he feared losing his arbitrary powers. The common man has borne the crushing burden of failed experiments. The constitution that was finally enforced in 1956 was neither democratic nor federal. It artificially created a ‘parity’ between the numerically divergent eastern and western wings of the country, denying the Bengalis their democratic right to rule based on the principle of majoritarianism. It also arbitrarily erased the western wing’s ethno-cultural diversity by forging a single province (One Unit), to weaken federalism. But neither scheme worked. The ensuing political instability and palace intrigues toppled as many as five governments in just two-and-a-half years, making it easier for a scheming and ambitious president to fold up the entire system, putting the country under the first martial law in 1958. The second exercise in political engineering was no less disastrous. The 1962 constitution was conceived by Gen Ayub Khan. He was ably assisted, among others, by a bevy of ambitious technocrats and unscrupulous judges. Retaining the ill-conceived One Unit and parity, he introduced a presidential system that denied universal adult franchise and sought ‘legitimacy’ from local governments — the basic democrats — which being malleable elected him and his loyalists to the federal and provincial legislatures. Interestingly, believing that it went against the ‘genius’ of the people, he dispensed with parliamentary democracy — something that India had successfully instituted years before in 1950. No wonder, the so-called ‘decade of development’ sowed most of the ills that continue to bedevil the political system to this day in the form of authoritarian masquerades, judicial kowtowing, electoral manipulation, ineffectual legislatures, crony capitalism, feudal empowerment, war-mongering, class inequalities, and the erstwhile east-west disparity. And small wonder that the sham democracy collapsed when protests swept the country in 1969 — another martial law was enforced, civil war broke out and half the country seceded in 1971. The 1973 Constitution — the third, in 26 years — has been the only compact that nearly reflected the ‘will of the people’, though it was framed by a post-1971 ‘rump’ parliament. The Constitution was almost consensual because the political leadership enjoyed a considerable degree of latitude in the post-1971 interregnum when the security establishment lay low. As a result, the Constitution cured much of the earlier ills, providing a fairly workable federal democracy. It included a parliamentary form of governance, a trichotomous balance of power, incremental autonomy for the provinces, fundamental rights and a fair amount of judicial independence. Above all, it recognised the people as the ultimate repository of political power and ‘trustees’ of sovereign authority. Thus, a solid foundation was laid for an institutional democracy. Had it been allowed to flourish, the country would have had a mature, stable and rules-based democratic order. But it was not to be. The elder Bhutto’s authoritarian streak, the opposition’s myopic vision and combative style, and a resurgent security establishment waiting in the wings, collectively brought down the constitutional dispensation in just four years. In 1977, the country again saw martial law. This time, the dictator sent an elected prime minister to the gallows. Since then, the polity has been turned into a petri dish of political engineering, a kaleidoscopic permutation of polities — naked martial laws, rule by a ‘troika’, ‘controlled’ democracy, imported rulers, dummy governments, a ‘hybrid’ model, and so on. Ironically, all these failed experiments were billed as ‘solutions’ to systemic problems. In reality, they were organised ‘institutional’ attempts to thwart constitutional democracy. All along, vested interests thrived, while the common man bore the crushing burden of failed experiments. But alas, the polity is back on the petri dish. The proposed scheme of creating more provinces on the pretext of addressing ‘bad governance’ is another experiment to dodge legitimate constitutional governance. It is bound to fail being superimposed, fanciful and unmanageably disruptive. The solution lies in a federal democracy — that is the only system that can ensure good governance and devolution to the third tier of governance.
articles.author: Shahab Usto

articles.title: Divine-human dialogue
articles.content: THE Divine-human communication or experience has a range of mediums through which it takes place. It may start from a simple prayer or a moment of focus to a truly mystical or spiritual experience leading to a transforming impact, though we experience the Divine all around, day and night, directly or indirectly, through the manifestations of creation. What we wish to discuss here is that the Divine-human communication may be rooted in, and spring from, the personal experiences of common people, not necessarily of saints or sages. These encounters take place at a more spiritual level, mediated through sociocultural and intellectual contexts. These experiences then are interpreted through a particular language, and a symbolic system (called semiotics) needing interpretation (hermeneutics) at multiple levels. Since these are subtle topics, needing a lengthy discourse, they are not discussed here for reasons of space. Divine-human communication may be twin-directional: downward and upward (in a metaphorical, not a physical sense). The ‘downward’ communication may involve (Divine) inspiration, revelation, or by opening the ‘heart’ through divulging mysteries by the Divine as and when the Divine wishes. These may be specialised communications meant for a broader purpose, which have often been reserved for the prophets and inspired individuals, such as sages, saints and the enlightened few. It is generally believed that the Divine communications are underpinned through mediums (‘wasila’, Holy Quran 5:35) through, for example, angels (‘malaika’) and ‘al-ruh’ (19:17), in the case of Bibi Mariam. As God cannot be personified, He uses expressions and manifestations through which He expresses His wish or desire. Humans try to communicate with the Divine in many ways. The Quran mentions many words to express this downward communication, such as ‘anzalna’, ‘arsalna’. In Surah al-Qadr, the Divine speaks of ‘anzalna’, which literally means “We revealed” (97:1). The same surah, in its fourth verse, mentions ‘tanazzalul malaikatu war ruh’ (therein come down the angels, and the spirit (ruh). The literal word for ‘tanazzalu’ may be ‘descend’, indicating a spiritual descending or coming down, in a metaphorical sense. The Quran says, “It is not possible for a human being to have Allah communicate with them, except through inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger-angel to reveal whatever He wills… .” (42:51). Humans are not capable of reaching God on their own, but it is the Divine who calls through a medium (maybe called an ‘angel’) a person and blesses them with the secrets of life or what is known as revelation or opening or divulging of the Divine truths. This may be called the Divine Mercy, which becomes a bridge or a medium (‘wasta’) with the Divine. The upward communication, on the other hand, involves a communication from the people to the Divine. There may be many forms in which humans try to communicate with the Divine, such as forms of supplication, prayers, beseeching, or simply talking. Still other forms may be silent, such as ‘muraqaba’, reflection, contemplation, meditation and focused silent ‘zikr’. Varieties of ways have been mentioned in the Quran regarding how humans approach the Divine. In one of the verses, Allah says humans approach God through prayer and how He listens to them. “When My servants ask thee concerning Me, I am indeed close (to them); I listen to the prayer of every suppliant when he calleth on Me; let them also with a will listen to My call and believe in Me; that they may walk in the right way” (2:186). Allah also nar-rates how hum-ans approach Him in dire situations. “When trouble toucheth a man, He crieth unto Us (in all postures) lying down on his side, or sitting or standing. But when We have solved his trouble, he passeth on his way as if he had never cried to Us for a trouble that touched him. …” (10:12). What this shows is that humans approach God when they are often desperate. These experiences or encounters, termed by William James as “Varieties of religious experience” can be vastly different, yet in many ways, they are similar in terms of their impact on the life of those who undergo them. These experiences have been documented by many, including Muslim mystics. The Quran testifies to this nearness and says, “…We will show them Our signs in the universe [aafaq] and within themselves [fi anfusihim] until it becomes manifest to them… .” (41:53). Thus, Divine-human communications may take place at ordinary as well as privileged times, each creating an impact of its own kind. These may take place in a variety of ways; individual and private, clearer and subtle. The writer is an educationist with an interest in the study of religion and philosophy.
articles.author: Jan-e-Alam Khaki

articles.title: Raging fires
articles.content: FOURTEEN newborns did not need to be burned alive for us to realise how deep the rot runs here. There are equally if not more damning indictments of this decrepit system that play out daily in Thatta, Mastung, Rajanpur, Rawalakot and Bannu. But when babies are locked into a room on fire in Islamabad’s biggest public hospital, with no staff member in sight, there must be a reckoning. Immediate accountability is certainly necessary, but removing a health secretary here and there is an easy escape for those at a much higher pay grade. Accidents happen, but the perpetual immiseration and oppression of the masses is not an accident. It is by design. When the interior minister deliberately remarked that the ‘system has failed’ some weeks ago, he neglected to mention that this same system works very well for those with power and money. Once upon a time, as the peerless Arif Hasan documented, Pakistan’s militarised ruling class shared space and facilities with the ordinary masses. Take public universities, for instance. There were also communal parks, cinemas, and even basic health services. But now those with deep pockets and connections want nothing to do with the ‘public’ — neither the mass of people, nor the facilities that the latter use. This is precisely why incidents like the abomination at Pims take place — because no one who is influential is affected. And by extension, nothing is done to fix what was broken a long time ago. This isn’t just a question of political will on the part of a callous ruling class. This is not just a question of political will on the part of a callous ruling class. It extends to our intellectuals as well. For decades, privatisation has been depicted as a panacea for all our economic problems. But no one bothers to acknowledge that the state has steadily withdrawn from whatever measly service delivery it once performed and left the mass of people to their own devices. The a priori insistence that ‘privatisation’ will somehow unequivocally turn out better for the ‘public’ at large is politically irresponsible. Let there be no mistake; this anti-people system needs the people to function. Who else will till the fields, serve the high and mighty in their homes and offices, construct the palatial mansions in which rulers live, and become soldiers in endless, bloody wars? Even when there are bad PR events like babies dying in pathetic public hospitals, the news cycle quickly moves on. Just like it did soon after the brutal demolitions of Islamabad’s katchi abadis and historical villages that left tens of thousands of people homeless. That was no accident any more than the deliberate withdrawal from delivery of public services like health and education is no accident. It is not as if the masses’ welfare has ever been a major concern of those who rule. This is, after all, a system built by colonial masters to extract resources and subjugate the mass of people. Its basic character has remained unchanged for eight decades. But for the first three decades after 1947, a left-wing politics of the people forced the state to make some concessions to the public interest. The establishment and its hangers-on have been unfettered by such an expansive, countrywide politics since the 1980s. And systematic and systemic dispossession of the masses is now the only game in town. The other, insidious side of the story is that a militarised ruling class that is enjoying ever-growing concentrations of wealth and power also acts out the role of concerned patron as a form of legitimation. Servitude has a long and deep history in the subcontinent, and both old and new moneyed classes revel in being able to dish out the carrot as well as the stick. Indeed, to be rich and powerful in Pakistan is arguably a much better deal than to be rich and powerful anywhere else in the world because of the total impunity that comes with class and state power. Some heads roll from time to time, mostly because of intra-elite palace intrigues. But in the final analysis, most of the big fish literally get away with murder. Violence and impunity run all the way down to the patriarchal household. The most recent example is that of the grotesque murder of Hina Javed. The alleged perpetrator is a university professor whose other family members have remained at large because of their suspected connections. The system is not failing its intended beneficiaries by any stretch of the imagination. And it will require much more than moral outrage to get rid of it. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
articles.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar

articles.title: Hospital tragedy
articles.content: WHERE does one begin? The mind goes first to the parents of the14 newbornswho died early Wednesday in the Mother and Child Health Ward of Islamabad’s Pims Hospital. The heart falters at the sheer scale of their loss. Their grief is shared across the country by people still struggling to comprehend how a tragedy of this magnitude was allowed to happen, and who must be held responsible. Multiple explanations have been offered for the fire: a short circuit, a spark, or an explosion involving an air-conditioning unit or its compressor. And every aspect of this incident unveils a new tragedy. Officials say the purified oxygen that should have been a lifeline for infants in respiratory distress instead accelerated the blaze dramatically. Within moments, the resulting inferno claimed the lives of 14 of the 15 babies in the ward. Eyewitnesses and parents described chaos: thick black smoke, shattered glass, locked or restricted doors, delayed rescue, and a near-total absence of proper evacuation protocols or functional fire-safety equipment. Some parents said they waited hours for help; official statements insisted fire tenders arrived within minutes of the emergency call. Rescue workers reported difficulty reaching the affected area. Hospital officials later acknowledged that the ward was routinely kept locked to prevent the theft of newborns. Clearly, there was no contingency plan for an emergency of this nature. And that, itself, is a damning indictment of the state of public hospitals. Equally frustrating has been the blame game that followed. Every stakeholder has been quick to point fingers even though few facts have been firmly established. The federal health secretary was swiftly suspended; scapegoated, many believe. But how far was he truly responsible? Is it fair, or even useful, to pin such disasters on individuals when the entire system remains broken? An inquiry committee has since been formed. That was necessary, and it is hoped that it will be able to diagnose the reasons that led to this tragedy. Yet, a much deeper reckoning is required. Removing a few officials will not prevent the next hospital fire. Pims is the largest and most prominent public hospital in the federal capital. It is the place where ordinary Pakistanis turn to in sickness, injury, and the hope of new life. Public hospitals in a country as populous as Pakistan need sustained resources and consistent support if they are to deliver even a basic standard of care and safety. Whether Pims ever received that support is a question that its administrators should be expected to answer. Until Pakistan stops chronically underspending on healthcare, the safety standards and quality of care in state-run hospitals cannot be expected to improve, and tragedies like this one will continue to claim lives. The bigger question is whether the authorities are ready to address that challenge.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Pipeline impasse
articles.content: THE Iran-Pakistan natural gas pipeline — a project decades in the making — is once again in the news. Lawmakers questioned the status of the stalled scheme in the Senate on Tuesday. As per the petroleum minister, the prime minister has formed a committee to find a “mutually acceptable” solution. It should be remembered that Iran has initiated arbitration proceedings in France, and Pakistan risks paying billions in penalty for not implementing the intergovernmental agreement. Pakistan’s dilemma is genuine: the country is stuck between arbitration and hefty penalties if it abandons the project, and potentially ‘secondary sanctions’ by the US if it goes ahead with it. However, considering that Iran completed its part of the pipeline in 2011, and the grace period provided to Pakistan to build its part expired in 2024, a solution should have already been found. Pakistan needs gas, and a steady supply from its western neighbour could address the shortages it faces. However, the issue here is more than one of logistics, project funding or gas pricing. It has fundamentally become a geopolitical concern, with the potential to spoil Pakistan-Iran relations unless handled carefully. On the other hand, American threats of sanctions cannot be ignored, keeping in mind Pakistan’s fragile economic situation. Instead of kicking the issue into the long grass, and waiting for a potentially adverse and expensive arbitration decision, Pakistan must address the pipeline question proactively. A comprehensive legal approach is required that protects national interests, while also maintaining a balance in ties with Iran and the US. One option would be to talk to the US and explain that any decision on the pipeline is best guided by Pakistan’s own economic interests. The Trump administration holds the current ruling set-up in Pakistan in high esteem and this aspect, coupled with Islamabad’s role as a mediator in the US-Iran conflict, can be leveraged to soften the American stance towards the project. Abandoning the pipeline would send the wrong message. The Iranians should also be kept in the loop to find a mutually beneficial way out. The destructive American and Israeli wars in the region will end one day. But Pakistan and its neighbours cannot change their geography, and must work to enhance friendship and trust.
articles.author: Editorial
